## The six framing scales {#six-ways-to-say-eu-framing .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.skiplink}
[Methods tutorial · 12 slides · skip to Hands-on 4 →](#hands-on-4-work-the-menu)
:::

::: {.small}
| Scale | Items | Claim predicts |
|---|---|---|
| `mcosmo` | peace · democracy · free movement · diversity · voice | negative |
| `mutil` | prosperity · social protection | negative |
| `mcomm` | unemployment · identity · crime · borders | **positive** |
| `mlib` | bureaucracy · waste of money | **positive** |
| `mpos` | all seven positive items | negative |
| `mneg` | all six negative items | **positive** |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The claim says "decrease positive dimensions" – `mpos` is the more literal reading, `mcosmo` is what was instructed. Across all six scales, the choice of outcome accounts for roughly **half** the variance in the grid as estimated, most of it because positive and negative framings take opposite signs. The disagreement between `mpos` and `mcosmo` accounts on its own for **0.15%**.
:::

::: notes
We start with the outcome. One survey question – what does the EU mean to you personally – offers thirteen response options, which the paper sorts into four scales. Cosmopolitan: peace, democracy, free movement, diversity, a stronger voice in the world. Utilitarian: prosperity and social protection. Communitarian: unemployment, loss of identity, crime, border control. Libertarian: bureaucracy and waste of money. And then two composites, all the positive items and all the negative ones. The third column trips people up, because for the negative framings the claim predicts a positive coefficient. [advance] The words of the claim itself are "decrease positive dimensions", which points at the composite rather than at cosmopolitan alone, yet on its own that disagreement accounts for less than one per cent of the variance in the grid. The choice among all six scales accounts for about half of it as estimated, more than all the other choices put together, and most of that half comes from positive and negative framings pointing in opposite directions. Once the framings are claim-aligned, the estimator accounts for more than the outcome does.
:::

## Building a scale – mean, sum or share {#building-a-scale-mean-sum-or-share .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Five binary items per respondent. Three defensible summaries:

- **Mean** of the five – a proportion between 0 and 1. Everyone contributes equally
- **Sum** – a count from 0 to 5. The same information on a different scale, which changes the size of the coefficient
- **Share** of all mentions – depends on how many options the respondent picked overall
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A **share** is relative to the respondent's own total, so somebody who ticked eight boxes contributes differently from somebody who ticked two. The mean and the sum do not depend on that total.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Among the five Multi100 analysts, one used a **mean**, one a **sum**, one a **share** and one three separate shares. Each choice is defensible, but no two of them measure the same quantity.
:::

::: notes
How do you turn five binary items into one number? There are three summaries, all defensible. The mean of the five, which gives you a proportion between nought and one and lets every item count equally. The sum, which is a count from nought to five: the same information on a different scale, so the coefficient will be five times bigger and mean the same thing. Or a share of all the respondent's mentions, which is what our panel uses, and the interesting one, because it is relative to how many boxes that person ticked overall. Somebody who ticked eight options contributes differently from somebody who ticked two. The mean and the sum do not work that way. And look at the fragment: among the five of us, one used a mean, one a sum, one a share, one three separate shares. All defensible, and not one of them the same quantity as the others.
:::

## Claim alignment {#claim-alignment-and-why-the-room-needs-it .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3"}
d$mcomm_ca <- 1 - d$mcomm      # reverse-code a negative framing

# now: negative coefficient = supports the claim, whatever the outcome
```

::: {.small}
Reverse-coding a bounded scale **flips the sign** of *b*, *t* and *r*, and leaves the magnitude, the standard error, the |t| and the p-value untouched. The same holds exactly for the beta family, since logit(1 − μ) = −logit(μ).
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your evidence stays the same, and only the sign convention in which it is reported changes.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
It is still an analytic decision, so it is set by an explicit `claim_align` switch in your preregistration, where a reader can find it.
:::

::: notes
Claim alignment was one of the ground rules for the menu, and it is what makes the class chart readable. If your outcome is one of the negative framings, you reverse-code it before fitting, as one minus the scale. What that does is flip the sign of the coefficient, the t and the partial r, and leave everything else where it was – the magnitude, the standard error, the absolute t, the p-value. And it holds exactly for the beta family too, because the logit of one minus mu is just minus the logit of mu. So nothing about your evidence changes, only the direction in which it is reported. But – and this is why we do it explicitly – it is still a real analytic decision, and a reader deserves to see it. That is why it is set by a visible claim-align switch in your preregistration block, where anyone reading the block will find it.
:::

## A bounded scale in a linear model {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Our outcome is a proportion. It lies strictly between 0 and 1, and its variance is smallest near the ends. A linear model assumes neither of those things.

- **Gaussian** – fit it as if it were unbounded. Simple and familiar, but it can in principle predict values outside 0–1
- **Beta** – a logit-link beta regression, built for bounded outcomes of this kind. It reports a **z** in place of a *t*
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Fitted as a beta regression, the baseline gives **b(logit) = −0.01399, z = −4.075, r = −0.258**, against **r = −0.242** from the gaussian fit, so the association keeps its direction and its significance and is marginally stronger.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The choice of distribution matters in principle, and on this claim it changes the result very little.
:::

::: notes
Next, the outcome family. Our outcome is a proportion – it lies strictly between nought and one, and its variance is necessarily smallest near the two ends, because a mean near zero cannot vary much. A linear model assumes neither of those things. So you have a choice. Gaussian treats it as if it were unbounded: simple, familiar, and in principle capable of predicting a framing score of one point two. Or beta regression with a logit link, which is built for bounded outcomes of this kind and reports a z instead of a t. Now the result. On this claim the two agree: the beta version of our baseline gives a logit coefficient of minus point zero one four, z of minus four point zero eight, partial r of minus point two six, against minus point two four from the gaussian fit. So the direction is the same, it is still significant, and it is marginally stronger. The distributional choice matters in principle, and here it changes very little.
:::

## The predictor – unemployment or GDP growth {#which-variable-carries-the-claim .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
The abstract says "poor economic performances". That names at least two things:

- **Unemployment rate** – what Task 2 of Multi100 instructed. Higher is worse
- **GDP growth** – what four of the five analysts used in their free phase, two of them beside unemployment. Higher is *better*, so the claim predicts a **positive** coefficient on positive framings
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Refitted on our panel, the free-phase model of analyst C6HJR (`mpos ~ growth + unemp`, two-way fixed effects) puts the growth coefficient at **b = +0.00167, t = 1.59**, in the direction predicted by the claim but not significant.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Across all the growth specifications in the grid, **70.5%** point in the direction predicted by the claim, but only **46.9%** are significant. Direction without significance is a different kind of support from the one that the unemployment specifications give.
:::

::: notes
Which variable is the claim actually about? The abstract says "poor economic performances", and that phrase names at least two different things. One is the unemployment rate, which is what Multi100 instructed in its second task and where higher means worse. The other is GDP growth, which is what four of the five of us reached for when we were free to choose, and where higher means better – so the claim predicts a positive coefficient on the positive framings, not a negative one. Refit my own free-phase model on this panel, the positive framings on growth and unemployment with two-way fixed effects, and the growth coefficient comes out at plus point zero zero one seven with a t of one point six: right direction, not significant. And across all the growth specifications in the grid, seventy per cent in the direction predicted by the claim but only forty-seven per cent significant. That is direction without significance, which is a materially different kind of support from what the unemployment specifications offer, and a reader deserves to be told which one they are getting.
:::

## Predictor form {#predictor-form-and-a-warning .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
- **Raw** `unemp` – a one-point rise in the rate
- **log(unemp)** – a proportional rise, so the step from 4% to 5% counts for more than the step from 20% to 21%
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Those two are genuinely different models and can give different answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
But **centring and standardising are not**. Subtracting a mean, or dividing by a standard deviation, is an *affine* change of scale: it moves the coefficient and its standard error by the same factor and leaves **t, r and p exactly unchanged**.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
For that reason the grid has no separate centred rows. A robustness check that varies only the centring is the same analysis restated.
:::

::: notes
Predictor form. Raw unemployment asks what a one-point rise in the rate does. Logged unemployment asks what a proportional rise does, which is a substantively different claim: it says the step from four per cent to five matters more than the step from twenty to twenty-one, and for something like unemployment that is quite plausible. Those two are genuinely different models and they can give different answers. But now the warning. Centring and standardising are not. Subtracting a mean, or dividing by a standard deviation, is an affine change of scale: it moves the coefficient and its standard error by exactly the same factor, so the t, the partial r and the p-value are untouched. That is why our grid contains no separate centred rows at all. If you come across a robustness check that varies only the centring, it is the same analysis written differently.
:::

## Four ways to handle countries and years {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
| Estimator | What it compares | What it assumes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pooled, clustered SE** | countries with each other *and* over time | no unobserved country differences |
| **Country FE** | each country with itself over time | country differences are stable |
| **Two-way FE** | the same, net of EU-wide year shocks | shocks hit everyone alike |
| **Random effects** | a weighted blend of both comparisons | country effects uncorrelated with the predictor |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The four estimators address different questions. A pooled estimate is about whether *high-unemployment countries* frame the EU differently, a fixed-effects estimate about whether *a country frames it differently when its own rate rises*.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Of the 41 cosmopolitan specifications with the wrong sign, opposite to the one that the claim predicts, **33 are pooled**.
:::

::: notes
Four estimators, and the thing to hold on to is that they do not answer the same question. Pooled with clustered standard errors compares countries with each other and with themselves at once, and assumes there is nothing systematically different about countries that you have not measured – which for twenty-seven European states is a strong assumption. Country fixed effects compare each country only with itself over time, which means every stable national difference drops out. Two-way fixed effects do the same and additionally soak up anything that hit all of Europe in a given year. Random effects blend the two comparisons, weighting by precision, and assume the country effects are uncorrelated with your predictor. Now the fragment: pooled asks whether high-unemployment countries frame the EU differently, and fixed effects ask whether a country frames it differently when its own rate rises. And in the grid, thirty-three of the forty-one wrong-sign specifications are pooled.
:::

## What fixed effects adjust for {#what-fixed-effects-actually-buy-you .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
**Absorbed**

- Anything stable about a country over the decade – institutions, history, size, prior EU sentiment
- Anything common to a year across all countries – the crisis itself, a treaty, a media cycle
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.small}
**Not addressed**

- A confounder that **varies within a country over time** – a national bailout, a change of government
- **Reverse causation**: today's framing moving tomorrow's unemployment
- Measurement error, selection into the sample
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the same statement as the DAG from Hands-on 2. `adjustmentSets()` on its solid part, before any of the pale nodes is wired in, returns country and year, which are what two-way fixed effects absorb, so **the graph and the baseline model make the same claim.**
:::

::: notes
Fixed effects are often treated as a general remedy for confounding, so it is worth being precise about what they adjust for. They absorb anything stable about a country across the decade – institutions, history, size, whatever the country already thought about the EU in 2004. And they absorb anything common to a year across all countries: the crisis itself, a treaty, a Europe-wide media cycle. What they do not touch is anything that varies within a country over time, which is where the interesting confounders are – a national bailout programme, a change of government, a domestic scandal. They do nothing about reverse causation, where today's framing moves tomorrow's unemployment. And nothing about measurement error or selection. Then the fragment: run adjustmentSets on the solid part of the graph from Hands-on 2, before you wired in any of the pale nodes, and it returns country and year. The graph and the baseline model are making the same claim.
:::

## The copredictor {#copredictor-control-or-second-exposure .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Put GDP growth in beside unemployment and you have made a choice you should be able to name:

- **As a confounder** – a slump raises unemployment *and* sours sentiment in the same year. Adjusting closes a back-door path that your fixed effects leave open
- **As a rival exposure** – growth is a second measure of the same "poor economic performance". Now you are asking which of the two the claim is about
- **As a mediator** – if unemployment works *through* growth, adjusting removes part of the effect you wanted
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The line of code is the same in all three cases, but each reading of it targets a different estimand. And remember the **Table 2 fallacy**, which is to read every coefficient in a regression table as a causal effect. The growth coefficient in that model is not automatically the causal effect of growth.
:::

::: notes
The copredictor axis looks like the most innocuous choice on the menu, and it is easy to get wrong. If you put GDP growth into the model beside unemployment, you have made a choice, and you should be able to say which one. You might mean it as a confounder: a slump raises unemployment and sours sentiment in the same year, so adjusting for growth closes a back-door path that your fixed effects cannot reach, because it varies within country over time. Or you might mean it as a rival exposure – growth is another measure of the same poor economic performance, and you are now asking which of the two the claim is really about. Or, if unemployment works partly through growth, growth is a mediator and adjusting for it removes part of the very effect you set out to measure. It is the same line of code with three different estimands. And do not forget the Table 2 fallacy: the growth coefficient in that model is not automatically the causal effect of growth.
:::

## Sample restrictions {#sample-which-countries-which-years .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
- **All** – 2004–2013, 27 countries, 270 cells
- **2004–2008** vs **2009–2013** – before and during. The split halves your data and tests whether the relationship is a crisis phenomenon
- **No bailout countries** – drop the cells where an EU/IMF programme was running
- **No Greece and Spain** – drop the two extreme unemployment trajectories
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The last two exclusions test whether the association depends on a handful of extreme cases, which would be a reason for concern. In this grid, **24 of the 41 wrong-sign specifications** come from samples that leave out the bailout countries.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
An exclusion is a claim about **who the finding is meant to be about**, and so it is a question about the estimand.
:::

::: notes
Sample. All years is the baseline. Splitting into 2004 to 2008 and 2009 to 2013 halves your data and asks a real question: is this a crisis phenomenon or a standing relationship? Then two exclusions. Drop the countries while an EU or IMF programme was running. Or drop Greece and Spain, whose unemployment trajectories are so extreme they could plausibly drive the whole thing on their own. Those last two are the interesting ones, because they test whether the association depends on a handful of extreme cases, which would be a reason for concern. On this claim there is some cause for it: twenty-four of the forty-one wrong-sign specifications sit in samples that leave out the bailout countries. An exclusion is also a claim about who your finding is meant to be about, which makes it a question about the estimand.
:::

## Weights {#weights-whose-country-year-counts-more .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Each cell is a mean of very different numbers of respondents. Weighting by `n_cy` makes a cell built from 2,000 people count for more than one built from 500.

- **Unweighted** – every country-year is one observation. You are studying *countries*
- **Weighted by `n_cy`** – cells count in proportion to the people behind them. You are closer to studying *people*
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
That changes the estimand, which is why the weight is one of the fourteen axes of the menu, beside the outcome and the estimator.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Practical note: random effects are never fitted with weights in the grid – the combination is not well defined for this design, so those rows do not exist.
:::

::: notes
Weights. Each cell in the panel is a mean over a very different number of respondents, so weighting by that count says a country-year built from two thousand people should count for more than one built from five hundred. That sounds like a purely technical refinement, but it changes what you are studying. Unweighted, every country-year is one observation and you are studying countries – Malta counts as much as Germany. Weighted, cells count in proportion to the people behind them, and you have moved a long way towards studying people. That is a change of estimand, which is why in this course the weight is one of the fourteen axes of the menu, chosen like the outcome or the estimator, instead of being left as an argument to the fitting function. One practical note: random effects are never fitted with weights in our grid, because the combination is not well defined for this design, so those rows simply do not exist.
:::

## Making the axes comparable {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
A coefficient from a beta model on a share and one from a weighted pooled model on a sum are not on the same scale. Multi100 and this course put them on one scale in three steps:

- Take the test statistic and its degrees of freedom
- Convert to a **partial correlation** *r* – the association between predictor and outcome, net of everything else in the model, on a fixed −1 to +1 scale
- Apply **claim alignment**, so the sign means the same thing everywhere
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Every specification in the class, and all 840 in the grid, can then be placed on one axis. `submit_exploration()` in Task 4 and `report_result()` in Task 5 do the conversion for you.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes numbers **comparable**, not **equivalent**. Two analyses that estimate different quantities remain different after the conversion, even when they are plotted side by side.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Silberzahn's teams faced the same problem: four of the twenty-nine reported a correlation or a standardised difference rather than an odds ratio. The authors converted everything to one scale and reported the **median**. A median summarises the estimates in one number, where a curve shows their whole distribution, and which of the two you want depends on what you mean to say next.
:::

::: notes
Last, the conversion that puts every result on the class chart. A coefficient from a beta model on a share and one from a weighted pooled model on a sum are not on the same scale, so an axis that holds both tells you nothing. Multi100, and this course after it, take the test statistic and its degrees of freedom, convert them to a partial correlation, and then apply claim alignment so that the sign means the same thing everywhere. A partial r is the association between predictor and outcome net of everything else in the model, on a fixed scale from minus one to plus one, and submit underscore exploration and report underscore result do the conversion for you. Comparable is not the same as equivalent, though. Two analyses that estimate different quantities remain different once they sit side by side, which is the estimand problem from the red-card study again. Silberzahn and colleagues faced the same difficulty when four of their twenty-nine teams reported something other than an odds ratio. They converted everything to one scale and reported the median, which gives one number where a curve gives the whole distribution.
:::
